## Notes on Ezra 10:23–44

**Verses 18–44 as a whole (the list)**
- Gill says the list names men who married foreign wives and then sent them away. He sorts them the way rabbinic writers sorted Jews: priests (v. 20), Levites including singers and gatekeepers (vv. 23–24), and ordinary Israelites (the rest). He adds that we know nothing more about these men. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/ezra/10-19.html
- Keil & Delitzsch use the same three groups: priests (vv. 18–22), Levites (vv. 23–24) and laymen (vv. 25–43). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezra-10.html
- Guzik's chapter summary on Enduring Word says the list shows the reform was thorough: even religious leaders were held to account, whatever their rank. Note that the site labels this summary as AI-generated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
- Matthew Henry notes that the people who should have taught the law broke it themselves, and their example made others bolder. But they repented, promised to send their wives away, and offered the ram the law required as a guilt offering. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-44.html
- Constable points out that no prophet in the text says whether God approved the plan. He still thinks it was God's will, partly because the inspired writer gives two chapters to it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezra-10.html

**v. 23**
- Utley says these are the same Levite groups found in the Ezra 2 list (2:40–42). No temple servants (Nethinim) or descendants of Solomon's servants appear among the guilty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/ezra-10.html
- BibleHub's study notes say the Levites helped the priests and looked after the temple. They give the meanings "Yahweh has bestowed" for Jozabad and "hearing" for Shimei. The teaching point they draw is that spiritual leaders matter when a community returns to God. https://biblehub.com/study/ezra/10-23.htm
- BibleHub's cross-references link this Jozabad with Nehemiah 11:16. There a Jozabad is a chief Levite overseeing the outside work of God's house. The page does not say whether it is the same man. https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-23.htm

**v. 24**
- Gill counts the singer and the gatekeepers ("porters") among the Levites. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/ezra/10-19.html
- Enduring Word's summary points out that singers are on the list as a sign of how thorough the reform was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/

**v. 25**
- Kretzmann (Lutheran) calls "Israel" here the lay members of the congregation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/ezra-10.html
- BibleHub's notes say the phrase shows repentance was not just for priests and Levites; ordinary Israelites were held to account too (they cite Numbers 15:29). https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-25.htm
- The Cambridge Bible (on Ezra 2:3) says Parosh is an odd name meaning "flea." Members of this family married foreign wives (10:25) and also helped rebuild the walls (Nehemiah 3:25). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-3.htm

**vv. 25–43 (the lay families)**
- The Cambridge Bible notes that the families in this list (Parosh, Elam, Zattu, Bebai, Bani, Pahath-moab, Harim, Hashum, Nebo) also appear in the Ezra 2 list of returnees. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/2-3.htm

**v. 26**
- Guzik notes that Shechaniah, the man who proposed the covenant in 10:2, was from Elam. He seems not to have married a foreign wife himself, but his father and uncles apparently had (10:26). He still stood with the guilty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/

**vv. 34–42**
- Keil & Delitzsch think the 27 men under Bani and Binnui probably came from various places in Judah, not from one household. They mention Bertheau's idea that "Bigvai" originally stood in one of these places in the text. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezra-10.html

**v. 44**
- *Numbers.* Barnes counts 113 guilty men: 4 from the high priest's family, 13 other priests, 10 Levites and 86 laymen from at least 10 families. He adds that the children made Ezra's task harder. Gill also gives about 113. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-44.htm
- *Small number, important men.* Benson quotes Dodd: the number is small compared with all the returnees, but these were prominent men whose example would have spread the problem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-44.htm
- *Why mention children? Commentators disagree.*
  - Poole and Benson think the phrase means most of the wives had no children. They see this as God's providence, showing His displeasure and making the separation less difficult. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-44.htm
  - Clarke thinks it shows only a few had children, and also how strictly the law was enforced. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/ezra-10.html
  - Keil & Delitzsch and the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary say it shows how thoroughly the reform was carried out. Sending away a mother of shared children is much harder than parting from a childless wife. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezra-10.html ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezra-10.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the fact is implied in Shechaniah's proposal (v. 3) but stated plainly only here. Terms were harder to settle where the marriage had produced children. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-44.htm
- *Were the children sent away too?*
  - Gill thinks they were not. Ezra's order (v. 11) does not mention them, so Gill supposes they were raised in the true religion and later received as converts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-44.htm
  - Matthew Henry says it is unclear, but it seems they were not. He thinks the wives were probably provided for according to their rank. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-44.html
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) takes the opposite view: wives and children were all sent away. He calls the step cruel and harsh but necessary for Israel's survival. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-44.html
- *Guzik on the children (from 10:3).* Guzik notes that Adeney thought including the children was too much zeal. Guzik disagrees and thinks it was God's will. He cites Yamauchi: mothers normally kept their children when a marriage ended. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-10/
- *A harsh critic.* The Expositor's Bible (W. F. Adeney) is very hard on Shechaniah's proposal, calling it something only a "fanatic" could call hope. Yet he admits Israel might not have survived as a Church, or kept its religion pure, without staying separate. His lesson: God must come first, even when the dearest human ties are wrecked. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezra-10.html
- *Geneva Bible.* Its note says the children were illegitimate because the marriages were unlawful. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-44.htm
- *The fix did not last.*
  - Keil & Delitzsch: the people swore again in Nehemiah 10:31. About 25–30 years later Nehemiah found such marriages again, including a high priest's grandson married to Sanballat's daughter (Nehemiah 13). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-44.htm
  - Henry: such corruptions creep in easily and are hard to clear out (Nehemiah 13:23; Malachi 2:11). Only the Redeemer will finally turn ungodliness from Jacob. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-44.html
  - The Light of Israel commentary quotes Wiersbe's image: you can pull the nails out, but the holes stay. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/10-43.html
- *Is this a model for divorce today?* Ligonier says this is narrative, and people in narratives are not always right. It admits the community may have erred. But because Ezra is portrayed positively, it thinks the divorces were more likely right. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/putting-away-the-foreign-wives . BibleHub's Q&A says this was a one-time crisis and should not become a general rule for ending marriages. https://biblehub.com/q/how_does_ezra_10_10_align_with_anti-divorce.htm . GotQuestions notes the event happened under the Law of Moses, in an earlier dispensation. https://www.gotquestions.org/abandon-foreign-wives-children.html

**v. 44 – the Hebrew is unclear (scholarship)**
- The Cambridge Bible says the clause is full of difficulties. Read literally, the Hebrew pronouns are masculine, as if the men bore the children. The Greek Septuagint says "they begat sons of them," while the Latin Vulgate says some of the wives had borne children. 1 Esdras 9:36 says they sent the wives away with their children, which hints at a different original text. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-44.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch reject changing the text. They argue the Septuagint already had today's wording and that 1 Esdras is only guessing from the context. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/10-44.htm
- The NET Bible note says the verse is hard in both grammar and meaning and may have been corrupted in copying. One proposed reading is "they sent these wives and children away." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Ezra+10%3A18-44
- The translations reflect this split. The NRSV, NAB (a Catholic translation) and Good News say the wives and children were sent away. The Douay-Rheims (also Catholic) says only that some wives had borne children. https://biblehub.com/ezra/10-44.htm
- Bible Odyssey (Katherine Southwood's approach) reads Ezra 9–10, including 10:44, as building up a sense of ethnic difference between the returned exiles (the "Holy Seed") and the "people of the land." It says the two groups were originally one people, and that many other Old Testament texts do not object to intermarriage the way Ezra and Nehemiah do. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/intermarriage-in-ezra-nehemiah/

**Where Protestant traditions differ:** I found no clear split between traditions on these verses. The real disagreements were between individual teachers. Commentators disagree on whether the children were sent away: Gill and Henry say probably not, Smith says yes. They also disagree on whether the whole action was right: Guzik, Constable and Ligonier say yes, while Adeney is critical and Ligonier admits it might have been wrong. Kretzmann (Lutheran) was the only tradition-specific voice I found, and he only explains the wording. I found nothing from Wesleyan, Pentecostal, Anglican or other Lutheran sources on this passage.
